The height of the gray bar therefore represents the per-kWh savings from load flexibility. 3.3 Technical Potential The total hourly load impacts from price response can be quantified in several different ways. These results are all for the full technical potential of price response, assuming 100% adoption of load flexible technologies, selection of dynamic prices, and price response. First, we look at the effective amount of Shed demand response incurred from price response, as shown in 35 Figure 20. As discussed in Section 2.5, effective shed looks at the hours of the year when demand response programs are most likely to be called and determines the average load impact from price response in those hours. As shown, results are quite similar across price scenarios, with Mild tariff values being slightly lower due to fewer times when price differentials make up for the cost of thermal losses. Across all years, crop irrigation and pool pumps each contribute about 500 GW of load shed potential. EV shed potential is quite low in 2019, as few customers had adopted EVs at the time, but by 2030 an expected 2 GW of effective shed is available from shifting these charging loads. Space cooling loads Residential water heating shed potential is relatively small, at about 170 MW, but this end use is expected to provide year- round value that is not represented by this metric. This is even more true for space heating, which has effectively no demand coincident with the system peak, and therefore no shed potential. Figure 20. Technical Potential, quantified as Effective Shed, across end uses and price scenarios Next, we look at the aggregate avoided costs to the grid from the modeled price response. Most of the avoided cost comes from space cooling, as hourly avoided costs are very concentrated in the hours of peak demand (as described in Section 2.5) which occur in the summer evenings when cooling loads have the largest impact. In 2030, EV charging price response contributes a similar amount of avoided costs to cooling loads. Pool pumps, crop irrigation, and water heating all contribute to avoided costs as well, while space heating is not significant for avoiding system costs. 36 Figure 21. Technical Potential, quantified by estimated avoided system costs, across end uses and price scenarios Bill savings, on the other hand, vary significantly across price scenarios. While customers can save $6B (in 2024 dollars) in 2030 on the Full tariff (Low price scenario), they are limited to only $1.25B in savings on the mild tariff. In the high scenario, electricity prices are much higher, and savings potential is correspondingly about twice the low scenario.
